problem_plain: The Riemann zeta function is a famous function whose 'zeros' (the inputs where it equals zero) control how the prime numbers are spread out. The Riemann Hypothesis says every interesting zero sits exactly on one vertical line, real part 1/2, in a strip running from 0 to 1. The quasi-Riemann hypothesis asks for much less: is there a fixed safety margin, some vertical line strictly left of the edge at 1, past which no zero ever appears, however high up you go? Until now nobody could rule out zeros creeping arbitrarily close to that right-hand edge.
why_it_matters: Zeros near the edge at real part 1 are what spoil our control of prime numbers. A fixed zero-free margin gives power-saving error terms for primes, including primes in arithmetic progressions, and it settles long-standing consequences such as Vinogradov's least-quadratic-nonresidue conjecture and a deterministic fast way to take square roots modulo a prime.

history.fact: Dirichlet (1837) introduced the character L-series to prove there are infinitely many primes in every reduced arithmetic progression.
Riemann's 1859 memoir related the zeros of zeta to the distribution of primes and formulated the critical-line conjecture (the Riemann Hypothesis, Re s = 1/2).
Hadamard and de la Vallee Poussin independently proved in 1896 that zeta has no zeros on the line Re s = 1, which gives the prime number theorem.

Classical zero-free regions (de la Vallee Poussin style) shrink toward the line Re s = 1 as the height or conductor grows, and for Dirichlet L-functions they can allow one exceptional real zero (a Landau-Siegel zero); so they never gave a fixed half-plane.
Zero-density estimates (e.g. Guth and Maynard's large-value estimates for zeta) bound how many zeros lie right of a line, but do not exclude every zero.
Before this work, no fixed sigma_0 < 1 with zeta(s) != 0 for Re s > sigma_0 was known; the quasi-Riemann hypothesis was open (the Riemann Hypothesis itself remains open, a Clay Millennium Problem).
history.source: paper intro (problem formulated as open, cites BCSS, FG); general knowledge (high confidence)

claim_precise: Main paper (OpenAI, 30 Sept 2026), Theorem 1.1: every finite-order Hecke L-function over F = Q(sqrt(-3)) has no zero in the open half-plane Re s > 7/8, and the same holds for every Dirichlet L-function, including zeta(s) (the pole at s=1 of principal characters allowed). Hence every nontrivial zero of zeta has real part at most 7/8 (by the functional equation, nontrivial zeros of primitive Dirichlet L-functions lie in 1/8 <= Re s <= 7/8), uniformly in character, conductor and height; in particular no exceptional (Landau-Siegel) real zero exists in (7/8, 1). Corollary: the least quadratic nonresidue mod p is at most C(log p)^A (e.g. A = 32), proving Vinogradov's conjecture n(p) << p^delta, and square roots mod p can be computed deterministically in time polynomial in log p. The proof has two stages: first a zero-free half-plane Re s > 11/12, then a refinement to 7/8. A companion paper (5 Oct 2026, written with human assistance) isolates the 11/12 proof, adding a corollary that the prime counting error in arithmetic progressions is << x^{11/12} log x uniformly for q <= x. A related paper (1 Oct 2026) claims uniform exclusion of Landau-Siegel zeros: (1-beta) log q >= c for an absolute c > 0. These are AI-written preprints; the repository says results are at different stages of verification, and this paper is listed in the Lean formalization catalogue.
claim_plain: The paper claims that zeta and all of its close cousins, the Dirichlet L-functions, have no zeros at all with real part bigger than 7/8. That gives a fixed zero-free margin of width 1/8 next to the edge, which settles the quasi-Riemann hypothesis. It does not prove the Riemann Hypothesis itself.
method_hint: Work over the Eisenstein integers Q(sqrt(-3)), compare two exact formulas for one sum built from cubic theta coefficients (one from a reflection formula, one from Poisson summation). If a zero sat too far right, the two sides would contradict each other. The first pass reaches 11/12, and a refined second pass pushes the bound to 7/8.

Do not say all zeros are on or near the critical line; zeros between 1/2 and 7/8 are not excluded.

The 7/8 bound is a strict open half-plane; the line Re s = 7/8 itself is not covered.

Do not say there was a previous numerical record for the half-plane; before this, no fixed sigma_0 < 1 was known (classical zero-free regions shrink toward Re s = 1).
The result is about zeta and Dirichlet L-functions (plus Hecke L-functions over Q(sqrt(-3))), not all L-functions.
The companion 11/12 paper is noted as written with human assistance; the main 7/8 paper is not.

problem_plain: Pi is irrational, so no fraction equals it exactly, but some fractions get remarkably close: 22/7, and 355/113, which is right to six decimal places. The question is how close a fraction p/q can get compared with the size of its denominator. A simple pigeonhole argument shows that for any irrational number you can always find infinitely many fractions within about 1/q^2. The "irrationality exponent" asks whether a number ever does a lot better than that: can you keep finding fractions within 1/q^3, or 1/q^2.5? If not, the exponent is 2, the smallest value possible, and the number is "as badly approximable as a typical number" in this sense.
why_it_matters: For seventy years nobody could rule out pi having occasional freakishly good fraction approximations; the best proven bound was still about 7.1. Settling it at exactly 2 also answers the Flint-Hills series question, a well-known puzzle about whether a particular sum built from sin(n) converges.

history.fact: Pigeonhole (Dirichlet) gives irrationality exponent at least 2 for every irrational number; 2 was the expected (conjectured) value for pi, recorded e.g. by Waldschmidt (Open Diophantine problems, 2004).
history.source: paper introduction, main.tex lines ~55-62; bib year 2004

history.fact: Mahler (1953) first proved pi has a finite irrationality exponent: explicit bound 42 for all denominators q>=2, with an eventual improvement to 30.
history.source: main.tex intro, 'Quantitative approximation and related work'

history.fact: Mignotte (1974) refined this to 21 (all denominators) and 20 eventually.
Salikhov (2008, see also 2010): mu(pi) <= 7.606308...
Zeilberger and Zudilin (2020): mu(pi) <= 7.103205334137..., the standard record before 2026.
Bai's September 2026 preprint claims mu(pi) < 7.101862832357.
Flint-Hills series sum 1/(n^3 sin^2 n), popularized by Pickover: Alekseyev (2011) showed convergence would require mu(pi) <= 5/2; Meiburg (2022) proved mu(pi) < 5/2 suffices for convergence.

Carella (2022) claimed exponent two (and more); the paper says that claim is not used and points out a sign error in the displayed proof of the stronger assertion. A 2025 convergence claim by Mantzakouras and Lopez Zapata was withdrawn in September 2026.

Almost every real number (in the measure sense) has irrationality exponent 2 (Khintchine), and Roth's theorem (1955) gives exponent 2 for every algebraic irrational; e is also known to have exponent 2 via its continued fraction.
history.source: general knowledge (high confidence); paper cites Roth 1960 ICM account

claim_precise: Theorem 1.1: The irrationality exponent of pi is 2. Precisely, for every real nu > 2 there is an integer Q(nu) such that |pi - p/q| >= q^(-nu) for all integers p and all integers q >= Q(nu). The threshold Q(nu) depends on nu and is NOT effective (the proof does not compute it). This is weaker than a uniform bound c/q^2 (equivalently, bounded continued-fraction partial quotients), which the paper does not claim. Corollary: the Flint-Hills series sum_{n>=1} 1/(n^3 sin^2 n) (radians) converges, via Meiburg's criterion mu(pi) < 5/2. More generally sum 1/(n^a |sin n|^b) converges iff a > max{1, b}. Status: OpenAI AI-generated preprint dated September 24, 2026; the repo includes a Lean formalization (lean/docs/017.md) whose scope is the exponent-2 statement; the Flint-Hills corollary is outside the formalized statement.
claim_plain: The paper claims to prove that pi is no easier to approximate by fractions than a typical number: for any exponent above 2, only finitely many fractions p/q get within 1/q^exponent of pi. As a consequence, it claims the famous Flint-Hills series sum of 1/(n^3 sin^2 n) converges.
method_hint: Assume pi had unusually good fraction approximations, use several of them to build a huge nonzero determinant from carefully interpolated polynomials (via the exponential/logarithm curve, since e^(2 pi i) = 1), then show the determinant must be both at least about 1 (it is a nonzero number with controlled denominators) and impossibly tiny, a contradiction.
overclaim_pitfalls: Do not say pi's continued fraction has bounded terms or that |pi - p/q| > c/q^2 for a fixed c; the paper explicitly does NOT claim this.
Do not say the proof gives an explicit/computable bound; the threshold Q(nu) is ineffective.
Do not say it proves pi is irrational or transcendental (known since 1761 and 1882).
Do not say 'no fraction can ever approximate pi well' - infinitely many fractions are within 1/q^2 (e.g. 355/113); the claim is only that you can't beat exponent 2 infinitely often.

Do not present it as peer-reviewed or universally accepted; it is an AI-generated preprint (Sept 2026), though the main statement has a Lean formalization in the repo. The Flint-Hills corollary is not part of the Lean scope.
Do not say it builds on the 7.103 bound; the paper says prior quantitative bounds are context, not inputs.
Do not credit it as the first claim of exponent 2: Carella (2022) claimed it, though the paper finds problems in that work's stronger argument and does not rely on it.
Flint-Hills: say 'converges', do not give a numerical value for the sum.

problem_plain: Take a needle one unit long and imagine a shape that holds a copy of it pointing in every possible direction. A Kakeya set is any such shape. In 1928 Besicovitch showed these sets can be strangely thin: in the plane one can have zero area. The Kakeya conjecture says they still can't be "thin" in the sense of dimension. A Kakeya set in n-dimensional space should be fully n-dimensional, even when its volume is zero. A stronger version, the "maximal" conjecture, asks for a quantitative estimate: thin tubes pointing in different directions can't overlap too heavily.
why_it_matters: Kakeya is a central open problem in harmonic analysis. The way thin tubes overlap governs deep questions in Fourier analysis (Fefferman's 1971 ball-multiplier counterexample, restriction theory), so progress here has consequences well beyond geometry. The 3D set case was settled by humans only in 2025. Four dimensions and the stronger maximal form were still open.

history.fact: The needle-turning problem goes back to Kakeya's era; the early convex formulation appears in Fujiwara and Kakeya, 1917.
Besicovitch (1928) constructed sets containing a unit segment in every direction with measure zero; the needle can be turned around in arbitrarily small area (Besicovitch 1928, Davies 1971).
Davies (1971) proved full Hausdorff dimension (2) for Kakeya sets in the plane; Cordoba (1977) gave the planar maximal estimate.
Wolff (1995) 'hairbrush' argument: Kakeya sets in R^n have Hausdorff dimension at least (n+2)/2, i.e. 5/2 in 3D and 3 in 4D.
3D improvements: Katz, Laba, Tao (2000) beat 5/2 for upper Minkowski dimension; Katz and Zahl (2019) beat 5/2 for Hausdorff dimension.

The 3D Kakeya SET conjecture (Hausdorff and Minkowski dimension 3) was proved by Hong Wang and Joshua Zahl, preprint 2025 (after their sticky case in 2022 and Assouad case in 2024); Guth, Wang, Zahl later streamlined it. This is human work and the 3D AI paper builds on it.
Wang and Zahl's set theorem gives a weaker dependence on density (lambda^{K(epsilon)}); getting lambda^3, which the maximal conjecture needs, was explicitly flagged after their theorem.

Best previous 4D Hausdorff bounds: Laba and Tao (2001) got Minkowski dimension above 3; for compact sets, Guth and Zahl (2018) with Zahl and Katz and Rogers (2018) got 3 + 1/40; Katz and Zahl's planebrush (2021) got Hausdorff dimension at least 3.059 (maximal-function parameter 3.049); Borges, Chan, Chen, Liu, Xi, Zhan (2025) raised the maximal parameter to (159+sqrt145)/56, about 3.0543.

claim_precise: Paper 1 (OpenAI preprint, Sept 23 2026) claims the 3D Kakeya maximal conjecture. Let K_delta f(omega) be the supremum over positions of the average of |f| over a unit-length tube of radius delta pointing in direction omega. Then for every epsilon>0, ||K_delta f||_{L^3(S^2)} <= C_epsilon delta^{-epsilon} ||f||_{L^3(R^3)} for all 0<delta<1. Equivalently, shaded delta-tubes satisfy |union Y(T)| >~ delta^epsilon lambda^3 sum|T| with the sharp cubic density power, uniformly in the density lambda. It builds on Wang and Zahl's 3D set theorem, via the Guth, Wang, Zahl union estimate. Paper 2 (OpenAI preprint, Sept 24 2026) claims the 4D Hausdorff-dimension Kakeya conjecture: any K in R^4 containing a unit segment in every direction has Hausdorff dimension 4. There are no compactness, measurability, or stickiness assumptions. It does NOT claim the 4D maximal conjecture. It uses a lemma from the 3D paper. Both are AI-generated preprints, not peer reviewed.
claim_plain: Two AI-written preprints claim to settle two open cases of the Kakeya problem. One is the stronger "maximal" version in 3 dimensions: tubes in different directions can't pile up too much. The other is the dimension version in 4 dimensions: any 4D set with a needle in every direction is fully four-dimensional.
method_hint: The proofs work by contradiction. Assume there is a worst-case tube arrangement and zoom in across scales: in 3D the tubes are forced into flat "plates" with a rigid, self-similar profile, and an information-entropy argument then rules that profile out. In 4D the line pieces are fitted with local quadratic "charts" that can be refined endlessly until a contradiction appears.

problem_plain: Take a geometric shape defined by polynomial equations, for example a doughnut-like shape with many holes in higher dimensions. Topology gives it a big list of "holes", or cohomology classes. Some of those classes are actually traced out by smaller shapes sitting inside it, which are themselves cut out by polynomial equations (these are called algebraic cycles). The Hodge conjecture says that every class with a certain symmetry, called a "Hodge class", comes from such polynomial pieces, possibly combined with fractional (rational) coefficients. In other words, a purely analytic test should be enough to detect what is genuinely algebraic.
why_it_matters: The Hodge conjecture is one of the seven Clay Millennium Prize problems and a central open question linking topology, analysis and algebraic geometry. CM abelian varieties are the most symmetric, arithmetic case. Earlier work (Milne) had shown that settling them would also settle the Tate conjecture for abelian varieties over finite fields and the Hodge standard conjecture for abelian varieties.

history.fact: Hodge posed the problem in his 1950 International Congress address (published 1952).
history.source: K3 products paper, history.tex; CM paper intro cites Hodge1952 p.184

history.fact: Codimension one (divisors) is already known: the Lefschetz (1,1) theorem. So for any abelian variety, products of divisor classes are automatically algebraic. The hard part is the Hodge classes that are not built from divisors.
Lefschetz proved the (1,1) theorem around 1924.
Weil classes are Hodge classes that are not generated by divisors. Moonen and Zarhin (1999) showed that this already happens on abelian fourfolds.
history.source: CM paper intro, cites MoonenZarhin1999 Thm 0.1

history.fact: Deligne (1982) proved that every Hodge class on an abelian variety is 'absolute Hodge'. This is an arithmetic property that algebraic classes share, but it does not produce algebraic cycles.
history.source: CM paper intro, cites Deligne1982 Main Thm 2.11

history.fact: Deligne and Andre reduced Hodge classes on CM abelian varieties to 'split Weil classes' on auxiliary CM abelian varieties, as formulated in Milne 2022. This said which classes would suffice, but it did not make them algebraic in all dimensions.
history.source: CM paper intro, cites Deligne1982, Andre1992, Milne2022 Thm 1

history.fact: Hazama (2003) reduced the problem to relations involving four labels and to codimension-two classes. Gao and Ullmo (2026) gave equivalent quadratic relations, but their conclusion concerned periods, not algebraic cycles.
history.source: CM paper intro, cites Hazama2003CM Thm 7.13 / Cor 7.14.1, GaoUllmo2026

history.fact: Markman (2025) proved that Weil classes on certain abelian sixfolds of Weil type are algebraic, and deduced the Hodge conjecture for all abelian fourfolds.
history.source: CM paper intro, cites Markman2025Secant Thm 1.5.1, Cor 1.6.1

history.fact: Milne (1999, 2002) proved that the Hodge conjecture for CM abelian varieties would imply the Tate conjecture for abelian varieties over finite fields and the Hodge standard conjecture for abelian varieties.
history.source: CM paper intro and 07-consequences.tex, cites Milne1999Tate, Milne2002Polarizations

history.fact: K3 side: Kuga and Satake attached an abelian variety to a K3 surface, and Deligne used this in his proof of the Weil conjectures for K3 surfaces. Buskin proved that rational Hodge isometries between K3 surfaces are algebraic. Earlier work (Ramon Mari, Varesco, Paranjape, Schlickewei) handled special cases and families.

claim_precise:
Main paper ('The rational Hodge conjecture for CM abelian varieties', OpenAI, Sept 30 2026, preprint). Theorem: let A be any complex abelian variety of CM type, meaning End(A)⊗Q contains a commutative semisimple Q-algebra of dimension 2·dim A. Then for every p ≥ 0 the Betti cycle-class map CH^p(A)_Q → H^{2p}(A,Q) ∩ H^{p,p}(A) is surjective. So the rational Hodge conjecture holds in every dimension and codimension, including for products and powers of CM abelian varieties.

Corollaries, obtained through Hazama/Abdulali and Milne's earlier conditional theorems:
(1) the generalized Hodge conjecture (Grothendieck's corrected version) for CM abelian varieties;
(2) the Tate conjecture for every abelian variety over a finite field, all codimensions, rational coefficients;
(3) the Hodge standard conjecture for abelian varieties over any algebraically closed field, any characteristic.

Proof strategy:
- Reduce to balanced four-factor tensors satisfying v1+v2=v3+v4.
- Realize each such tensor by mapping a single algebraic surface into four CM abelian varieties, which needs a nonzero 'surface period'.
- Build that period from theta one-forms on compact quotients of the complex 2-ball (unitary signature (2,1)).
- Use Hecke/Frobenius slope arguments to pin down the CM types.

Companion preprints in the family: rational Hodge for every finite product of projective complex K3 surfaces (Oct 4 2026), with no conditions on Picard number or endomorphism field; and algebraicity of the Kuga–Satake correspondence for every projective complex K3 surface (Oct 3 2026).

All of these are AI-generated preprints. The repository says its results are at different stages of verification, and this family is not Lean-formalized.
claim_plain: The preprint claims to prove the Hodge conjecture completely for one important, highly symmetric class of shapes: abelian varieties with "complex multiplication", in every dimension. Using known earlier implications by Milne, this would also settle two famous related conjectures for abelian varieties: the Tate conjecture over finite fields and Grothendieck's Hodge standard conjecture. Companion preprints claim the same kind of result for any product of K3 surfaces.
method_hint: Every Hodge class is broken into simple four-piece "balanced" building blocks. Each block is then made algebraic by finding one surface that maps to four special abelian varieties and has a nonzero period integral, built from theta functions on a ball quotient.
overclaim_pitfalls: Do NOT say it 'solves the Hodge conjecture' or 'wins the Millennium Prize'. It is a special case: CM abelian varieties (plus K3 products in companion papers). The general conjecture remains open.
Do NOT say it proves Hodge for all abelian varieties. Only CM ones are covered (non-CM abelian fourfolds were handled by Markman 2025, a human result).

The Tate conjecture and standard conjecture consequences hold only for abelian varieties (Tate: over finite fields). They come from Milne's earlier implications, not from new arguments for general varieties.
These are AI-generated preprints, not yet peer-reviewed, and not Lean-formalized. Say 'the paper claims' or 'the preprint proves', not 'it is now established'.
The 'rational' qualifier matters: rational (fractional) coefficients are allowed. The integral Hodge conjecture is false in general.
Deligne's 1982 'absolute Hodge' theorem did not prove algebraicity. Do not credit earlier work with more than it did.
The first-known case of non-divisor Hodge classes was found by Moonen–Zarhin in 1999. Do not claim these are new phenomena.

problem_plain: Picture a network where every node has to pick a "color" (a label) out of a big palette, and every link carries a rule like "whatever color you pick, your neighbor must pick exactly this matching color." Each choice forces exactly one answer next door, which is why these are called "unique games." The Unique Games Conjecture says that even when you are promised that almost every rule (say 99%) can be satisfied at once, no efficient algorithm can tell that apart from a network where hardly any rules can be satisfied (say 1%), unless P = NP.
why_it_matters: The conjecture has been one of the biggest open problems in theoretical computer science since 2002, because if it is true, then many textbook approximation algorithms (Max-Cut's 0.878 and Vertex Cover's factor 2, among others) are provably the best possible unless P = NP. Settling it would pin down exactly how well whole families of hard optimization problems can be approximated.

history.fact: Subhash Khot introduced the Unique Games Conjecture in 2002.
history.source: UGT paper intro (00-introduction.tex, 'Khot introduced the Unique Games Conjecture in 2002')

history.fact: Goemans and Williamson (1995) gave a semidefinite-programming algorithm for Max-Cut with approximation ratio alpha_GW = 0.878567...
Before this work, the best unconditional NP-hardness for Max-Cut ruled out ratios above 16/17 (Hastad's theorem plus gadgets of Trevisan-Sorkin-Sudan-Williamson).
Khot, Kindler, Mossel and O'Donnell (2007) showed alpha_GW is optimal for Max-Cut assuming the UGC, using the Majority Is Stablest theorem of Mossel-O'Donnell-Oleszkiewicz.

Vertex Cover: a maximal matching gives factor 2 (folklore). Prior unconditional hardness: Hastad below 7/6 (2001); Dinur-Safra below 10*sqrt(5)-21 ~ 1.36068 (2005); the 2-to-2 Games program culminating in Khot-Minzer-Safra's expansion theorem (2018) gave hardness below sqrt(2).
Khot and Regev (2008) showed Vertex Cover is hard to approximate below factor 2 assuming the UGC.
history.source: Vertex Cover paper history.tex; UGT paper 07-consequences.tex

history.fact: The 2017-2018 2-to-2 Games Theorem (Khot, Minzer, Safra; Dinur, Khot, Kindler, Minzer, Safra; Barak, Kothari, Steurer) gave a Unique Games gap with completeness near one half and arbitrarily small soundness; getting completeness near one was a separate, open problem.
history.source: UGT paper intro, 'Grassmann expansion and the completeness obstacle'

history.fact: Known algorithms (Trevisan 2008; Charikar-Makarychev-Makarychev 2006; Arora-Barak-Steurer 2010 subexponential-time) and integrality gaps (Khot-Vishnoi) did not refute the conjecture; Arora-Barak-Steurer's algorithm is subexponential, not polynomial.
The repository reports a Lean formalization covering the Unique Games reduction statement and the Max-Cut, Vertex Cover, Min-UnCut and directed feedback vertex set results.

claim_precise: Main preprint ("The Unique Games Theorem", OpenAI, Sept 23 2026): For every fixed epsilon, delta in (0, 1/2), there is an integer s and a deterministic polynomial-time reduction from 3SAT to explicit unweighted Unique Games instances over the alphabet K = F_2^s such that satisfiable formulas give value >= 1 - epsilon and unsatisfiable formulas give value <= delta. The graph is simple and bipartite, and every constraint is a translation a(v) = a(u) + c. The paper says this resolves the UGC positively in its usual edge-value form (Khot 2010, Conj. 2.5). Plugged into earlier conditional reductions by other authors (KKMO, Khot-Regev, Raghavendra, etc.), it turns their UG-conditional thresholds into NP-hardness. Companion preprints also give direct proofs that do not go through the UGT: NP-hardness of approximating Max-Cut within any fixed ratio above alpha_GW ~ 0.87856 on simple unweighted graphs; NP-hardness of Vertex Cover within any fixed factor below 2 (the YES case has cover < (1/2 + 1/m)n, the NO case > (1 - 1/m)n); and NP-hardness of approximating Min-UnCut and directed feedback vertex set within any fixed constant factor. The direct proofs rely only on established PCP and Label Cover hardness. All are AI-generated preprints, and the repository lists Lean formalizations for these statements.
claim_plain: The preprint claims a proof of Khot's Unique Games Conjecture: assuming P is not equal to NP, no fast algorithm can tell nearly fully satisfiable unique games apart from almost unsatisfiable ones. Companion papers separately claim to prove directly that the classic Max-Cut ratio of 0.878 and the factor 2 for Vertex Cover cannot be beaten by any fixed margin unless P = NP.

problem_plain: Take any convex shape, like a square, a disk or a triangle, centred at the origin. Every such shape has a 'dual' or 'polar' shape: the set of directions y with x·y ≤ 1 for every point x of the original. Making the shape bigger makes its polar smaller, so the product of the two volumes doesn't change under stretching. The disk gets the largest possible product (π² in the plane, a classical theorem). Mahler asked the opposite question in the late 1930s: which shape makes this product as small as possible, in every dimension?
why_it_matters: Mahler's question is one of the best-known open problems in convex geometry. It is tied to the geometry of numbers, and more recently to symplectic geometry (the "phase space" of classical mechanics). The planar case was settled by Mahler himself and the 3D symmetric case only came in 2020, so a proof in every dimension, with the equality cases included, would be a landmark.

history.fact: Mahler introduced the volume-product problem through his work on transference in the geometry of numbers (1939), and proved the planar inequality himself (polygon paper, late 1930s; cited as 1938 in one companion paper and 1939 in the other).
history.source: symmetric paper introduction.tex 'History and context'; general paper 00-introduction.tex

history.fact: Reisner showed that the planar symmetric minimizers are exactly parallelograms (1986). Meyer completed the planar general case in 1991: triangles are exactly the minimizers.

Saint-Raymond proved the sharp symmetric inequality for unconditional bodies, those symmetric under every coordinate sign flip (1981). Meyer (1986) and Reisner (1987) identified the Hanner equality cases in that class. Reisner proved it for zonoids (1985/1986).

Bourgain and Milman (1987) proved the 'reverse Santalo' bound: correct up to a factor c^n, but without the sharp constant. Kuperberg (2008) gave an explicit, better constant using Gauss linking integrals. Nazarov (2012) gave a complex-analytic proof.

Meyer and Reisner (2006) proved the sharp nonsymmetric inequality for polytopes with at most n+3 vertices. Kim and Reisner (2011) showed simplices are strict local minimizers. Nazarov, Petrov, Ryabogin and Zvavitch (2010) showed the cube is a strict local minimizer, and Kim (2014) extended this to all Hanner polytopes.

Iriyeh and Shibata proved the full 3-dimensional symmetric case, including equality (published 2020). A 2026 preprint by Chen, Li, Xi and Xu proves the 3-dimensional general case, P(K) ≥ 64/9 with tetrahedra as the only minimizers.

Symplectic link: Artstein-Avidan, Karasev and Ostrover (2014) tied the symmetric Mahler conjecture to Viterbo's volume-capacity conjecture. They proved that the Hofer-Zehnder capacity of K x K° equals 4. Haim-Kislev and Ostrover disproved the unrestricted Viterbo conjecture (2025) using a non-symmetric example.
The maximum of the volume product is reached by ellipsoids (the Blaschke-Santalo inequality). The open question was only the minimum.

problem_plain: Imagine painting every single point of an infinite flat sheet of paper, with one rule: any two points exactly one inch apart must get different colors. What is the smallest number of paint colors that makes this possible? That number is called the chromatic number of the plane, and the question is known as the Hadwiger-Nelson problem.
why_it_matters: It is one of the most famous easy-to-state open problems in geometry and combinatorics. For nearly 70 years the answer was only known to be somewhere between 4 and 7, and the lower bound only moved once, in 2018.

history.fact: The problem dates to Edward Nelson in 1950; Nelson got the lower bound 4 and John Isbell found the upper bound 7 using a hexagonal coloring (unpublished observations, recounted by Soifer 2003).
Hadwiger's published formulation (1961) gives the bounds 4 and 7.
The Moser spindle (Moser & Moser, 1961): a 7-point unit-distance graph that cannot be 3-colored, giving a small finite proof that at least 4 colors are needed.
The lower bound stayed at 4 until Aubrey de Grey (2018) built a finite unit-distance graph that cannot be 4-colored, so at least 5 colors are needed. His corrected graph has 1,581 vertices.

Follow-up work shrank such graphs: Heule (2018) found 553-vertex examples via SAT solvers; Parts (2020) found a 509-vertex graph and a human-verifiable proof; Exoo and Ismailescu (2020) gave an alternative proof of the bound 5.

If color regions must be measurable (not arbitrarily wild), Falconer (1981) already proved at least 5 colors are needed. For 'nice' map-like colorings, Townsend (1981/2005) proved at least 6, and Sokolov and Voronov (2025) proved at least 7 for polygonal colorings.
So before this paper, for completely unrestricted colorings, the known range was 5 to 7.

The repository's Lean docs state the formalization covers 'no proper five-coloring' (arbitrary colorings) and the 7-color upper bound.

problem_plain: Multiplying two n-by-n matrices (grids of numbers) the schoolbook way takes about n^3 multiplications: every row meets every column. The question is how much faster it can be done as the matrices get huge. Mathematicians measure this with one number, omega: the smallest exponent such that multiplication takes about n^omega operations. We know omega is at least 2, because you have to write down all n^2 entries of the answer, and at most 3, from the schoolbook method. Where it actually sits between 2 and 3 is one of the central open problems in algorithms.
why_it_matters: Matrix multiplication sits underneath much of computing: solving linear systems, determinants, matrix inversion and many graph algorithms all inherit its exponent. Any bound on omega becomes a bound for all of these. Since 1990, decades of work had moved the record only from about 2.3755 to about 2.3712, so a drop to 2.25 would be a very large step.

history.fact: Strassen (1969) found a 2x2 algorithm using 7 multiplications instead of 8; applied recursively this gives omega <= log2(7), about 2.807, the first sub-cubic algorithm.

history.fact: Key tools followed: Bini's approximate algorithms (1980), Schonhage's asymptotic sum inequality (1981), Strassen's laser method (1986-87) and asymptotic spectrum of tensors (1988).
Coppersmith and Winograd (1990) combined tensor powers with progression-free sets; their analysis gave omega < 2.375477.
Higher-power refinements: Stothers (2010) and Davie-Stothers (2013), Vassilevska Williams (2012), Le Gall (2014); Alman-Vassilevska Williams refined laser method gave omega < 2.3728596 (SODA 2021).

Duan-Wu-Zhou (2023, asymmetric hashing), Vassilevska Williams-Xu-Xu-Zhou (2024), and Alman-Duan-Vassilevska Williams-Xu-Xu-Zhou (2025) pushed it further; the six-author work also gives dual exponent alpha >= 0.321334.

problem_plain: An arithmetic progression is a run of evenly spaced numbers, like 5, 12, 19, 26: start somewhere and keep adding the same step. Erdős asked how sparse a set of whole numbers can be and still be forced to contain such runs of every length. His proposed test was to add up the reciprocals of the numbers in the set (1/a for each a). If that sum goes to infinity, must the set contain evenly spaced runs of length 3, 4, 5, 100, and so on? The primes pass this test, since 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/5 + 1/7 + ... diverges.
why_it_matters: It is one of Erdős's best-known conjectures, open since he posed it in the 1970s, and it would contain both Szemerédi's theorem and the Green–Tao theorem on primes as special cases. Answering it needs much stronger bounds on progression-free sets than were known for long progressions; before this, they were known only for 3-term progressions.

history.fact: Erdős and Turán began studying the largest progression-free subsets of {1..N} in 1936 and conjectured r_3(N) = o(N).
Erdős posed the reciprocal-sum question (divergent sum of 1/a implies progressions of every finite length) as Problem 4.33.6 in Math. Balkanica 4 (1974).
Roth (1953) proved the 3-term density case, with r_3(N) << N/log log N; Szemerédi proved 4 terms in 1969 and all lengths in 1975 (positive-density sets contain arbitrarily long progressions).
Behrend (1946): a progression-free set can still have size about N exp(-C sqrt(log N)), so the answer can't be a power saving in N.
Green and Tao (2008, Annals): the primes contain arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions. The primes have divergent reciprocal sum, so they are a special case of Erdős's conjecture.

history.fact: Bloom and Sisask (arXiv 2020) proved r_3(N) << N/(log N)^{1+c}, which settled the 3-term case of the reciprocal-sum conjecture.

Kelley and Meka (2023) proved r_3(N) << N exp(-c (log N)^{1/12}). Bloom and Sisask (2023) improved the exponent to 1/9, and Raghavan (2026) reached about 1/6. All of these are for 3-term progressions only.

For longer progressions, Gowers (2001) proved r_k(N) << N/(log log N)^{c_k}, and Green–Tao (2017) proved r_4(N) << N/(log N)^c. Leng, Sah and Sawhney (2024) proved r_k(N) << N exp(-(log log N)^{c_k}) for all k ≥ 5. Their saving is only in log log N, which is too weak for Erdős's question.
Erdős attached a cash prize to this problem, commonly cited as $3000 and later $5000. It is listed as Erdős Problem #3.

Equivalently, an α-dense subset of [N] contains a k-term AP once log N ≥ A_k(2+log(1/α))^{A_k}, a threshold that is quasipolynomial in 1/α. Corollary (Erdős's conjecture): every A ⊆ ℕ with Σ 1/a = ∞ contains nonconstant APs of every finite length. The proof sums the density bound over dyadic blocks [2^m, 2^{m+1}), and the resulting series is summable. problem_plain: Take a group, meaning a collection of symmetries or moves you can combine, and build its "group algebra": formal sums of group elements that you add and multiply like polynomials. In ordinary numbers, a product of two nonzero things is never zero. Kaplansky's zero-divisor conjecture says this should also hold in the group algebra, as long as the group has no torsion, i.e. no move that returns you to the start after repeating it a few times. Put more simply: no torsion means no zero divisors.
why_it_matters: This is one of the best-known of Kaplansky's group-ring conjectures. The question goes back to Higman's 1940 thesis, it was proved for large classes of groups, and many people expected it to be true. A counterexample marks a hard limit on how far those positive results can reach.

history.fact: The question goes back to Graham Higman's 1940 thesis.
history.source: paper intro, build/paper.tex 'History and related constructions'

history.fact: Kaplansky posed it in a 1956 conference contribution, published in 1957 (Problem 6).
Torsion gives easy zero divisors. If g has order m>1, then (1-g)(1+g+...+g^{m-1})=0. The conjecture asks whether ruling out torsion is enough.

Higman (1940) proved it for groups in which every nontrivial subgroup maps onto Z. Kropholler, Linnell and Moody (1988) proved it for torsion-free elementary amenable groups. Fisher and Sanchez-Peralta (2026) proved it for torsion-free 3-manifold groups.

Rips and Segev (1987) built torsion-free groups without the 'unique product' property. That property would have forced the conjecture to hold for those groups, but losing it does not by itself produce a zero divisor.

Giles Gardam disproved the related Kaplansky UNIT conjecture over F_2 (paper published 2021), and later over the complex numbers (2024). That was a nontrivial unit, not a zero divisor, so the zero-divisor conjecture stayed open.

Family 197 (companion paper, Oct 4 2026) uses the same graph-and-cone method to build a finitely presented torsion-free group with a,b,c in F_2[G] where ab=1, ac=0 and c is nonzero. So ab=1 but ba is not 1, which breaks Kaplansky's direct-finiteness conjecture even without torsion. Elek and Szabo (2004) showed sofic groups are directly finite, so this group must be non-sofic. An earlier companion paper did characteristic two using a group with odd-order torsion.

The repository lists a Lean formalization of the full main theorem: finitely presented, torsion-free, finite 2D classifying space, and nonzero alpha, beta with alpha*beta=0 over ZMod 2. It is OAI.TorsionFreeZeroDivisors.main in lean/OAI/Algebra/GroupRing/Main.lean, and grep finds no 'sorry' in that directory.

claim_precise: Theorem 1.1: there exist a finitely presented torsion-free group G and nonzero elements α, β in F_2[G] (coefficients in the two-element field) with αβ = 0. Moreover, G admits a finite two-dimensional classifying space (K(G,1)). This disproves Kaplansky's zero-divisor conjecture: for K a field and G torsion-free, K[G] would have no nonzero zero divisors. The construction works over F_2, characteristic two. Companion family 197 uses the same method for a finitely presented torsion-free G with a, b, c in F_2[G], ab = 1, ac = 0, c ≠ 0, so ba ≠ 1. That disproves Kaplansky's direct-finiteness conjecture with a torsion-free group, and the group is necessarily non-sofic.
claim_plain: The paper builds an explicit kind of torsion-free group from randomly chosen finite graphs. In its group algebra with coefficients mod 2, two nonzero elements multiply to exactly zero. So Kaplansky's zero-divisor conjecture is false, at least over the field with two elements.
method_hint: Take two finite labelled graphs and glue a cone onto each, so every closed loop becomes trivial. Then α and β are sums over the graphs' vertices, and terms in αβ come in matching pairs. Every vertex in the pairing graph has odd degree, so each component has an even number of terms, and in mod-2 arithmetic they all cancel. The hard part is the two safeguards: showing α and β are not themselves zero, and showing the group has no torsion (asphericity). Both are proved through random-graph estimates and planar separation.
overclaim_pitfalls: Don't say it disproves Kaplansky's conjecture over every field or over the complex numbers. The counterexample is over F_2, characteristic 2. It disproves the conjecture as stated for all fields.
Don't confuse it with Gardam's 2021 counterexample to the UNIT conjecture. That was a different conjecture, and the units are not zero divisors.
Don't call it the first counterexample to any Kaplansky conjecture. Gardam disproved the unit conjecture first. This is the zero-divisor one.
The group is not 'random' in the final answer. Random graphs are used to show that suitable graphs exist, and the group is a specific finitely presented one.

problem_plain: Take the interval from 0 to 1 and stretch and squeeze it with zig-zag-free 'bent line' maps: each map is made of finitely many straight pieces, the bends happen only at dyadic points (like 1/2, 3/4, 5/8), and every slope is a power of 2 (1/2, 1, 2, 4...). Composing such maps gives a group called Thompson's group F. The question: is F 'amenable'? Roughly, a group is amenable if you can always find finite chunks of it whose boundary is tiny compared to their size, so the group can be 'averaged over' fairly; nonamenable groups (like free groups) always leak a constant fraction across their boundary, no matter how you choose the chunk.
why_it_matters: Whether F is amenable has been one of the most famous open problems in group theory since Geoghegan's 1979 conjecture, because F sits exactly on the fence: it dodges the standard test for nonamenability (it has no free subgroups) yet is not built from the obviously amenable groups either. It has attracted several published or circulated claimed solutions in both directions that turned out to have errors or remain contested.

history.fact: Richard Thompson introduced the group F in 1965; an early published construction appears in McKenzie and Thompson (1973).
Amenability via invariant means goes back to von Neumann (1929) and Day (1957); Folner's criterion (1955) characterizes it by finite sets with small relative boundary.
Ross Geoghegan conjectured in 1979 that F is nonamenable (recorded by Cannon, Floyd, and Parry, 1996).
Brin and Squier (1985) showed F contains no nonabelian free subgroup, so the classical free-subgroup obstruction to amenability does not apply.
F is not elementary amenable (Cannon-Floyd-Parry 1996), so it is not amenable for 'cheap' structural reasons either; neither fact settles the question.
Brown and Geoghegan (1984) showed F has a classifying space with finitely many cells in each dimension (strong finiteness).

Moore (2013) proved tower-type lower bounds on the size of any Folner sets for F and characterized amenability of F via a Ramsey-type property of finite binary trees; Haagerup and Olesen (2017) showed simplicity of the reduced C*-algebra of Thompson's group T would imply F is nonamenable; Guba (2025, 2026) gave further density and mean restrictions.

Prior claimed resolutions: Shavgulidze (2009) claimed amenability, with errors identified by Moore; Moore withdrew an amenability claim (2012) after Akhmedov found an error; Akhmedov's 2021 version claims nonamenability via a height-function criterion.
history.source: paper introduction.tex (Context and prior work, final para)

claim_precise: Theorem 1.1: Thompson's group F (increasing piecewise linear homeomorphisms of [0,1] with finitely many pieces, dyadic rational breakpoints, slopes in 2^Z, viewed as a discrete group) is not amenable, i.e. admits no positive normalized left-invariant mean on bounded real functions; equivalently, there is a finite set S in F and epsilon > 0 such that no nonempty finite A satisfies |hA delta A|/|A| < epsilon for all h in S. This confirms Geoghegan's 1979 conjecture. The repository also includes a Lean formalization whose scope note says it rules out such an invariant mean for the standard dyadic PL group (no explicit boundary constant or generating set given). problem_plain: Take a 2D flow where the velocity at every point (x, y) is given by polynomials, like water swirling on a tabletop. Some trajectories loop around forever in closed orbits. A "limit cycle" is an isolated loop: nearby trajectories spiral toward it or away from it, with no other loop right next to it. Hilbert's sixteenth problem (second part) asks how many such loops a polynomial flow of a given degree can have. The weaker "uniform" question is whether there is a ceiling at all: is there one maximum number of loops that works for every polynomial flow of degree d?
why_it_matters: It is one of Hilbert's 1900 problems and one of the least solved. A related claimed proof (Dulac, 1923) turned out to have a gap. Even for degree 2 (quadratic flows) nobody had proved that any finite ceiling exists. Limit cycles describe self-sustained oscillations such as heartbeats, predator-prey cycles and electronic oscillators.

history.fact: Hilbert posed the problem: the maximum number and arrangement of limit cycles of planar polynomial systems (Problem 16). The paper cites the 1902 English printing; the problem list itself is from 1900.
history.source: uniform paper 01-introduction.tex 'Historical context'; 1900 date is general knowledge (high confidence)

history.fact: Dulac claimed in 1923 that each individual polynomial field has finitely many limit cycles. Ilyashenko found a gap in that argument in 1985. Écalle and Ilyashenko gave proofs of individual finiteness around 1990-1992 using complex and asymptotic analysis of return maps.

Individual finiteness (each field has finitely many) is weaker than uniform boundedness (one bound depending only on the degree). Finiteness for every member of a family does not by itself bound the numbers as the coefficients vary.

Partial results on uniformity: Bautin (1952) showed at most 3 cycles bifurcate from a weak focus or center in quadratic systems. Ilyashenko and Yakovenko (1995) proved finite cyclicity for elementary polycycles in generic families, and Kaloshin (2003) made this explicit. Binyamini, Novikov and Yakovenko (2010) gave explicit bounds for the infinitesimal problem (zeros of Abelian integrals). Kaiser, Rolin and Speissegger (2009) obtained o-minimal and definability results.

Even for quadratic systems (degree 2), it was not previously known whether a uniform finite bound exists. Quadratic systems with 4 limit cycles have been known since about 1979-80 (Shi Songling; Chen and Wang).
history.source: general knowledge (high confidence); not stated in the paper

history.fact: Liénard systems x' = y - F(x), y' = -x: Lins, de Melo and Pugh (1977) conjectured at most floor((n-1)/2) limit cycles when deg F = n. Rychkov (1975) proved the bound of 2 for odd quintic F. Dumortier, Panazzolo and Roussarie (2007) found counterexamples with 4 cycles in degree 7. De Maesschalck and Dumortier (2011) found 4 cycles in degree 6. De Maesschalck and Huzak (2015) found at least n-2 cycles for every n >= 6. Li and Llibre (2012) proved at most 1 cycle in degree 4. Li and Lu (2014) bounded only the slow-fast limiting regime in degree 5. The general degree-5 case was described as open in an August 2026 preprint.
history.source: Liénard paper introduction.tex and references.tex (years from bibliography)

claim_precise: Paper 1 (Uniform bounds for planar polynomial limit cycles), Theorem 1.1: for each integer d >= 1 there is a finite integer B(d) such that every real planar polynomial vector field x' = P(x,y), y' = Q(x,y) of degree at most d has at most B(d) limit cycles in the whole plane. Cycles are counted as geometric images without multiplicity, and there are no restrictions on coefficients, cycle locations or stability. The paper calls this a positive resolution of the uniform boundedness assertion in the second part of Hilbert's 16th problem. It explicitly gives no effective formula for B(d), and it does not use individual finiteness (Dulac/Écalle/Ilyashenko) as a premise. Paper 2 (Two limit cycles for quintic Liénard systems), Theorem 1.1: if deg F <= 5, the system x' = y - F(x), y' = -x has at most two limit cycles in R^2, and some members have exactly two, so the exact maximum is 2. No parity or sign assumptions are made on F. This is the degree-5 case of the Lins-de Melo-Pugh conjecture. Verification status: the Lean formalization (lean/docs/143.md) covers only the quintic Liénard result. The uniform-bounds paper is not formalized and is an unrefereed AI-generated preprint.

It proves that the ceiling exists but does not compute it. A companion paper, checked in Lean, pins down one special family exactly: Liénard oscillators with a degree-5 damping term have at most 2 limit cycles, and 2 is achieved.
method_hint: Limit cycles near an orbit are the fixed points of a "return map" (follow a nearby trajectory once around). The proof splits each return into finitely many local passages and, using a degree-dependent finite geometric description plus asymptotic expansions on nested complex domains, turns the uniform bound into a finite-dimensional counting argument.

problem_plain: In quantum mechanics, measuring a system is like picking a set of perpendicular directions (a "basis") to measure along. Two such sets are "mutually unbiased" if knowing the outcome of one measurement tells you absolutely nothing about the other: every outcome comes out equally likely, like a position measurement against a momentum measurement. The question is how many measurement sets can all be unbiased with each other at once. In 6 dimensions (6 complex coordinates), nobody knew the answer: is it 3, 4, 5, or 7?
why_it_matters: Unbiased bases are the best measurement sets for working out an unknown quantum state, and they show up in quantum cryptography. Dimension 6 is the smallest dimension where the standard constructions break down, so it has been a well-known open problem in quantum information for over 30 years.

history.fact: Mutually unbiased bases (MUBs) trace back to Schwinger's unitary-operator framework (1960); Ivanovic studied quantum state determination with them (1981).
history.source: paper intro, introduction.tex 'Historical context and scope'

history.fact: Wootters and Fields (1989) showed that complete sets are optimal for state determination and built d+1 MUBs whenever the dimension d is a prime power. In any dimension d, at most d+1 MUBs can exist.

Dimension 6 = 2x3 is the first dimension that is not a prime power. Combining the 2-dimensional and 3-dimensional constructions (a tensor product) gives 3 MUBs in C^6 (Klappenecker and Rotteler, 2004).
history.source: paper intro, introduction.tex; Lemma 'Three mutually unbiased bases in dimension six'

history.fact: Zauner's conjecture that 3 is the maximum in dimension 6 goes back to his 1991 diploma thesis. His 1999 doctoral thesis has the related quantum-design conjecture, and N(6)=3 appears as Conjecture 1 in Klappenecker and Rotteler (2004).

Partial results: Grassl (2004) showed that the standard and Fourier pair cannot be part of 4 MUBs. Numerical searches by Butterley and Hall (2007) and by Brierley and Weigert (2008) supported the conjecture. Jaming, Matolcsi, Mora, Szollosi and Weiner (2009) used a certified computer discretization to rule out 4 MUBs that contain the standard basis plus any member of the two-parameter Fourier family.
Weiner's completion theorem (2013): any d MUBs in C^d extend to a complete set of d+1. So in dimension 6, ruling out 7 also rules out 6.
history.source: companion paper intro (Exact Fourier certificates), paper.tex

history.fact: Before these preprints, the known range was 3 <= N(6) <= 7. The upper bound 7 is just the general d+1 bound, and the companion cites Bandeira-Doppelbauer-Kunisky (2022) showing that one class of degree-6 relaxations cannot improve the bound of 7.
history.source: companion paper intro; d+1 bound in main intro; the 'previously 3 to 7' framing is general knowledge (high confidence)

claim_precise: Main preprint ("The maximum number of mutually unbiased bases in dimension six", OpenAI, Sept 24 2026). Theorem (computer-assisted): under the stated binary64 floating-point arithmetic and compiler conditions in its appendix, a fresh complete run of the documented verification pipeline certifies that no 4 pairwise mutually unbiased orthonormal bases exist in C^6. Together with the known tensor-product construction of 3 bases, this gives N(6)=3, which resolves Zauner's dimension-six MUB conjecture. The second basis (a complex Hadamard matrix) is arbitrary, not limited to any known family. A corollary: at most 3 pairwise Killing-orthogonal, adjoint-closed Cartan subalgebras exist in sl_6(C). Companion preprint ("Exact Fourier certificates for complex Hadamard matrices of order six"): (i) it proves the Matolcsi-Ruzsa-Weiner (2013) Fourier-vanishing conjecture: every order-6 complex Hadamard matrix not equivalent to Tao's cubic matrix S_6 has a vanishing character sum at every permutation of (1,1,1,-1,-1,-1). (ii) An exact certificate using only integer and rational arithmetic rules out 7 MUBs in C^6, so N(6) <= 5 by Weiner's completion theorem. This weaker bound does not depend on floating point.
claim_plain: The preprint claims to settle a 35-year-old question: in 6 dimensions you can fit exactly 3 mutually unbiased measurement sets, never 4. The "never 4" part is a large computer-assisted proof with rigorous error bounds. A companion paper uses exact arithmetic to give an independent, weaker bound: at most 5.

Inside each ball, collect every vector that could be unbiased to both bases, then show that the vectors cannot be arranged into two more full bases (two disjoint 6-cliques in a graph where all 36 cross pairs are unbiased).

problem_plain: Take a free group: all the words you can spell with some letters (say a, b) and their inverses, where nothing cancels except a letter next to its own inverse. From any group you can build a giant infinite-dimensional algebra of operators, its "group von Neumann algebra." The free group on 2 letters gives L(F2), on 3 letters L(F3), and so on. The question is whether these algebras are secretly the same. Does the number of letters survive the passage to the operator algebra, or does it get washed out?
why_it_matters: The question goes back to the founding of the subject in the 1940s and became one of the central open problems in classifying "finite factors." A whole field, Voiculescu's free probability, grew up partly as a tool to attack it.

history.fact: Free group factors arose in Murray and von Neumann's foundational work on rings of operators (1943). Their 'non-hyperfiniteness' showed they differ from the hyperfinite factor, but it did not tell different ranks apart.
history.source: paper intro, main.tex Introduction para 1 (cites murray_vonneumann1943, radulescu1992)

history.fact: The question of whether L(F_m) and L(F_n) are isomorphic for distinct m, n >= 2 is credited to Richard Kadison, per Dykema's historical account (1994).
history.source: paper intro, main.tex Introduction para 1 (cites dykema1994 p.123)

history.fact: Voiculescu developed free probability: reduced free products (1985) and semicircular/circular systems (1990). His compression results showed that the fundamental group of L(F_infinity) contains every positive rational.
Radulescu (1992) showed that the fundamental group of L(F_infinity) is all of the positive reals.
history.source: paper intro para 2; references.bib title of radulescu1992

history.fact: Dykema (1994) and Radulescu (1994) independently built 'interpolated' free group factors L(F_r) for every real r > 1 and proved the amplification formula L(F_s)^t = L(F_{1+(s-1)/t^2}). Together these give a dichotomy: either ALL the free group factors are isomorphic, or they are ALL pairwise different. Radulescu's version (1994) includes r = infinity.

Voiculescu asked whether free entropy dimension (Free entropy survey, 2002) depends only on the algebra and not on the chosen generators. A 'yes' would have shown the factors are different, since a free n-tuple has entropy dimension n.
The paper cites a recent 2026 preprint of Shlyakhtenko that identifies certain Fuchsian group factors with interpolated free group factors, and says it uses no result from that preprint.

claim_precise: The preprint "An isomorphism of the free group factors" (OpenAI, Sept 23 2026) claims Theorem 1.1: for every integer n >= 3 there is a unital, normal, trace-preserving *-isomorphism L(F_n) = L(F_{n+1}). Applying this at n=3 and n=4 gives L(F_3) = L(F_5). Amplifying by sqrt(2) with Dykema's formula N_s^t = N_{1+(s-1)/t^2} then gives Theorem 1.2: L(F_2) = L(F_3). It is an affirmative answer to the free group factor isomorphism problem. Combined with the classical Dykema–Radulescu dichotomy, Corollary: all interpolated free group factors L(F_r), 1 < r <= infinity, including L(F_infinity), are isomorphic, and their common fundamental group is R_{>0}. A further corollary answers Voiculescu's question in the negative: the free entropy dimensions delta, delta_0, delta^*, delta^star are not invariants of the algebra. Each takes every integer value n >= 2 on finite self-adjoint generating tuples of L(F_2). This is an AI-generated preprint. The repo lists a Lean comparator challenge (lean/docs/287.md) for the statement "all interpolated free group factors are isomorphic". The repo README cautions that results are at different stages of verification.
claim_plain: The paper claims the answer is YES: the free group factors are all the same. The algebra built from 2 free letters is isomorphic to the one built from 3, and by older results to every other rank, even infinitely many letters. problem_plain: Picture a flat metal plate of some shape whose edges are perfectly insulated, so no heat can leave. Heat it unevenly and let it settle. After a long time, the temperature pattern looks like one basic wave shape, the first non-trivial "Neumann eigenfunction". The hot spots question asks where the hottest and coldest points of that pattern end up. Do they always sit on the edge of the plate, or can one of them be stuck somewhere in the interior?
why_it_matters: This is a classic question linking heat flow, vibration modes, and the geometry of a shape. It is known to be false for some shapes with holes, so the open case was whether it always holds for shapes without holes in the plane. Many partial results covered only special families such as convex symmetric domains, lip domains, and triangles.

history.fact: The hot-spots problem came from Jeffrey Rauch's discussion of the long-time behavior of heat flow with insulated boundary (the paper cites Rauch's lecture published in 1975).
Rauch posed it around 1974 (lecture published 1975).
history.source: general knowledge (high confidence) that it is usually dated 1974

history.fact: Banuelos and Burdzy (1999) distinguished strict and nonstrict versions, and developed probabilistic coupling methods.

history.fact: Burdzy and Werner (1999) built a counterexample: a planar domain with two holes where the conjecture fails.
history.source: paper intro 'Background and methods'; bib BurdzyWerner1999

history.fact: Bass and Burdzy (2000) gave examples where both the max and min are strictly inside; Burdzy (2005) got failure with just one hole.
The conjecture for simply connected planar domains (no holes) is stated explicitly as Conjecture 1.2(ii) in Burdzy (2005).

Special cases proved: Jerison-Nadirashvili (2000) convex domains with two axes of symmetry; Pascu (2002) convex domains with one symmetry (antisymmetric eigenfunctions); Atar-Burdzy (2004) lip domains; Miyamoto (2007) certain nearly circular convex domains.
history.source: paper intro para 'Important geometric special cases'

The starting point of this paper is Rohleder's variational principle for tangent vector fields (2021 preprint, 2024).

claim_precise: Let Omega be a nonempty bounded simply connected open set in R^2 with C-infinity (smooth) boundary, and let mu be its first positive Neumann eigenvalue (often written mu_2 when the constant mode is counted first). Theorem 1.1: every nonzero u in the real eigenspace for mu has grad u(x) != 0 at every interior point x. Consequently min over the boundary of u < u(x) < max over the boundary of u for all interior x, so all global extrema lie on the boundary only (strict hot spots). No convexity or symmetry is assumed, and it holds for every eigenfunction even if the eigenvalue is multiple. The no-critical-point statement is stronger than boundary extrema, since it also rules out interior saddle points. The repo also says a Lean formalization of this main theorem exists (lean/docs/369.md, ComparatorChallenges/HotSpots.lean). It is an AI-generated (OpenAI) preprint dated September 24, 2026.
claim_plain: The paper claims that for any smooth plane shape without holes, the hottest and coldest points of the slowest-decaying insulated heat mode always lie on the edge, never inside. In fact that temperature pattern has no flat spot anywhere in the interior. This settles Burdzy's simply connected version of the hot spots conjecture for smooth domains.
method_hint: The Neumann condition makes the gradient of the eigenfunction tangent to the boundary. The proof builds an energy whose zero set is exactly these gradients, then constructs special boundary multipliers from a new Green-kernel positivity theorem. An interior critical point would then produce too many independent eigenfunctions, which is impossible in the plane.
overclaim_pitfalls: Do NOT say it proves the hot spots conjecture for all domains: it is false in general, since there are counterexamples with holes (Burdzy-Werner 1999, Burdzy 2005).

The result is for SMOOTH (C-infinity boundary) bounded simply connected PLANAR domains only. It does not cover domains with corners in general (triangles were done separately by Judge-Mondal), nor higher dimensions, nor non-smooth or Lipschitz domains.

It concerns the FIRST positive (second, counting the constant) Neumann eigenfunction, not all eigenfunctions or arbitrary heat solutions. For heat flow it describes long-time behavior for generic initial data.

problem_plain: Catalan's constant G = 1 - 1/9 + 1/25 - 1/49 + ... (alternating reciprocals of odd squares) is about 0.9160. The question is simple: is G a fraction of two whole numbers, or is it irrational like pi?
why_it_matters: G is one of the most famous constants whose irrationality has never been proved; it is a close cousin of zeta(3), which Apery famously proved irrational in 1979, but the same trick failed for G.

history.fact: Apery (1979) proved zeta(2) and zeta(3) irrational with recurrence-based approximations; Beukers (1979) gave integral proofs. Zudilin (2003) built Apery-like approximations for G, but the resulting integer forms do not shrink to zero, so they don't prove irrationality.

Rivoal and Zudilin (2003) proved at least one of beta(2)=G, beta(4), ..., beta(14) is irrational; later narrowed to beta(2)..beta(12) by Zudilin (2019) and to beta(2)..beta(10) by Lai and Zhou (2022) - but none pinned down G itself.
Calegari (2005) proved a 2-adic analogue of G irrational; Calegari-Dimitrov-Tang (2024) proved 1, pi^2, L(2,chi_-3) linearly independent - a related constant with conductor 3, not G.

claim_precise: Theorem 1.1: Catalan's constant G = beta(2) = sum_{j>=0} (-1)^j/(2j+1)^2 = L(2, chi_{-4}) is irrational. Proof is by contradiction: assuming G is rational, determinants Delta_N of size 48N (built from moments of two kernels, each a rational combination of 1, G, zeta(2), with zeta(2) cancelled via Taylor-contact Chebyshev rows) become rational; prime-by-prime denominator bounds give a lower bound on |Delta_N|, an integral formula gives an upper bound, and nonvanishing along large primes N=p is shown via Frobenius reduction to three fixed matrices checked by an exact finite certificate. The two bounds are incompatible. The paper notes Sun (2026) independently announced the same qualitative result.

problem_plain: A plasma, like the gas in a star or a fusion reactor, is a swarm of charged particles that rarely collide. They move through the electric and magnetic fields they create themselves, and those fields change as the particles move. The relativistic Vlasov–Maxwell equations describe this feedback loop, including particles moving close to the speed of light. The question is whether, starting from any smooth, reasonable initial state, the solution stays smooth forever, or whether it can break down in finite time, for example by some particles being pushed to unbounded momentum.
why_it_matters: Vlasov–Maxwell is the basic model of collisionless plasma physics. Whether its smooth solutions can blow up in 3D has been one of the central open problems in kinetic theory since Glassey and Strauss's work in the 1980s. The analogous problem for the simpler Vlasov–Poisson system, which has no magnetic field, was settled in the early 1990s.

history.fact: Wollman (1984) proved local-in-time existence and uniqueness of classical solutions.
history.source: paper introduction.tex, Historical context; references.bib year 1984

history.fact: Glassey and Strauss (1986) showed that a smooth solution continues as long as the particles' momentum support stays bounded. This is the continuation criterion. In 1987 they proved global existence for initially dilute (small) plasmas.
DiPerna and Lions (1989) proved global WEAK solutions for large data. These give no regularity or uniqueness. Rein (2004) gave a version for the relativistic one-species system.

Glassey and Schaeffer proved global classical existence in reduced dimensions: 1.5D (1990), 2.5D (1997) and the planar case (1998). Rein (1990) handled small perturbations of suitable global solutions.

New proofs and refinements of the continuation criterion include Klainerman–Staffilani (2002), Bouchut–Golse–Pallard (2003), Pallard (2005, 2015), Sospedra-Alfonso–Illner (2010) and Luk–Strain (2014, 2016). Luk–Strain (2014) showed it suffices to control the momentum support projected onto a 2D plane.

Small-data and small-particle results include Schaeffer (2004), Bigorgne (2020), Wei–Yang (2021, large fields but small particle density), Wang (2022) and Bigorgne (2025). All of them keep a particle-smallness assumption.
Wang (July 2026, two papers) proved large-data global existence for cylindrically symmetric data with no smallness assumption. This is a different data class: it requires symmetry.
For the simpler Vlasov–Poisson system (no magnetic field), global classical solutions in 3D were obtained by Pfaffelmoser (1992), and independently by Lions–Perthame around 1991.
history.source: Pfaffelmoser1992 is in references.bib; Lions–Perthame is general knowledge (high confidence)

claim_precise: Theorem 1.1 is about the 3D, one-species relativistic Vlasov–Maxwell system with no background charge. Take any smooth admissible datum: the initial density f0 is smooth, nonnegative and compactly supported in (x,v); the initial fields E0 and B0 are smooth with every spatial derivative bounded and are square-integrable (finite energy); and the constraints div E0 = rho and div B0 = 0 hold. Such a datum generates a unique global classical solution. On every finite interval [0,T], f, E and B are C^infinity, f has compact phase-space support (the momentum bound may grow with T), and the divergence constraints persist. The paper puts no size or symmetry restriction on the data and allows nonzero total charge. It describes this as resolving the large-data global classical regularity problem for this model. The key step is a bound on the signed momentum impulse of each particle. This bound gives a lower bound on the time needed for the maximal momentum to double, and those lower bounds have a divergent sum, so the momentum support cannot blow up in finite time. The Glassey–Strauss continuation criterion (as stated by Luk–Strain 2014) then gives global smoothness. The repository lists a Lean formalization of the main theorem, OAI.RVM.global_classical_solution, with a comparator configuration that permits only the standard axioms.
claim_plain: The paper claims that in three dimensions, a plasma described by the relativistic Vlasov–Maxwell equations never develops a singularity. For any smooth starting state with particles confined to a bounded region and finite field energy, the solution exists for all time, is unique, and stays smooth. No smallness or symmetry is assumed.
method_hint: The proof tracks the net (signed) push each particle receives over time, not the absolute size of the force. Cancellations in the light-cone geometry then show that particle momenta cannot double infinitely often in finite time, so they stay bounded and the classical continuation criterion applies.

Do not say it covers the non-relativistic (classical) Vlasov–Maxwell system or multi-species plasmas. The theorem is stated for the one-species relativistic model only.
Do not claim uniform-in-time bounds or decay. The momentum support is bounded on each finite time interval but may grow as T grows. The paper says nothing about scattering or long-time asymptotics.

Do not say it was the first large-data global result of any kind. Global weak solutions (DiPerna–Lions 1989) existed, and Wang (2026) handled large cylindrically symmetric data. The claimed novelty is classical (smooth) solutions for arbitrary data with no symmetry or smallness.

problem_plain: Given any polynomial equation with whole-number coefficients, like x^2 + y^2 = 3, is there a single computer program that can always tell you whether it has a solution in fractions (rational numbers)? Searching can find a solution if one exists, but it can never confirm that none exists.
why_it_matters: Hilbert asked the whole-number version in 1900, and it was answered in 1970. The fractions version stayed open for decades and is one of the best-known open problems in logic and number theory.

history.fact: Hilbert posed his tenth problem (whole-number solutions) in his 1900 list; Davis, Putnam and Robinson (1961) and Matiyasevich (1970) showed no algorithm exists for integer solutions.

Julia Robinson (1949) defined the integers inside the rationals with a first-order formula; later Poonen (2009) and Koenigsmann (2016) reduced the quantifiers needed, but none gave the purely existential definition that would settle the rational case directly.
In 2026, Koymans–Pagano and Alpöge–Bhargava–Ho–Shnidman settled the problem for rings of integers of number fields; the paper notes that this does not cover the field Q itself.

claim_precise: Theorem 1: no algorithm, given f in Z[X_1..X_n] with n part of the input, decides whether f has a zero in Q^n. Corollary: the set H10(Q) has Turing degree 0' (equal to the halting problem), and this still holds when inputs are restricted to polynomials of total degree at most four. The proof is a Turing reduction from integer solvability. For each f, an effectively generated sequence of finite tests is built, each answerable by rational-solvability queries, and f has an integer zero iff every test passes. It does not claim a Diophantine definition of Z in Q. It depends on companion results, including a 'pointwise 2-converse' for elliptic curves with rational 2-torsion (a companion preprint) and an odd regular Fontaine–Mazur theorem at 2.
claim_plain: The preprint claims a negative answer: no computer program can decide, for every polynomial equation with integer coefficients, whether it has a solution in fractions. It also claims the problem is exactly as hard as the halting problem.
overclaim_pitfalls: Don't say it proves the integers can be defined inside the rationals by polynomial equations. The paper says its route doesn't need that, and Mazur's conjecture would rule it out.
Don't present it as peer-reviewed or accepted. It is an AI-generated preprint whose proof relies on companion preprints.
Don't say Hilbert's original tenth problem was solved here. That was settled for integers in 1970 by Matiyasevich, building on Davis, Putnam and Robinson.
Don't say no individual equation can be solved. Many specific equations can be decided; the claim is only that no single algorithm handles every equation.
Don't attribute the 2026 number-field results (Koymans–Pagano; Alpöge–Bhargava–Ho–Shnidman) to this paper.
visual_ideas: A machine labeled 'Algorithm?' takes in a polynomial. On one side, a search sweeps outward over a grid of fractions p/q and lights up a dot when it finds a solution. On the other side, the search runs forever for an equation with no solution, and a large question mark appears.

method_hint: Integers are encoded as multiples nP of a point on a rank-one elliptic curve, and a height estimate forces these encoded integers to be ordinary, bounded integers. Together these turn integer solvability, already known to be undecidable, into a question about rational solutions.

problem_plain: Suppose you have a shape X, and when you multiply it by a line (X times a line) you get exactly ordinary 5-dimensional space. Zariski's cancellation problem asks whether you can then "cancel the line" and conclude that X itself has to be ordinary 4-dimensional space.
why_it_matters: It is one of the central questions about recognizing affine space, the most basic object in algebraic geometry. Over the complex numbers it was open in every dimension three and higher; the paper cites a July 2026 preprint that still lists it as open.

history.fact: Cancellation holds for the line (Abhyankar–Eakin–Heinzer, 1972) and for the complex plane (Fujita 1979; Miyanishi–Sugie 1980).
In positive characteristic, Neena Gupta showed cancellation fails, first for affine 3-space (Invent. Math. 2014) and then in every dimension at least 3 (Adv. Math. 2014).
Over the complex numbers (characteristic zero), dimensions 3 and up were still open, as noted in a July 2026 Gaifullin–Petrov preprint.

claim_precise: For P = C[p,s,u,F,J], x = s^2+u^3+p^2F, H = x^2F − (1+2sx)J − p^2J^2 − pu, the paper claims A = P/(H) is an integral 4-dimensional complex algebra with A[w] ≅ C^[5] but A ≇ C^[4]. So Zariski cancellation fails over C in dimension four. As corollaries, H is not a coordinate of C^[5] but becomes one after adding one variable, so the Stable Coordinate Conjecture fails in ambient dimension 5. Also, the maps p: Spec A → A^1 and (p,H): A^5 → A^2 are smooth A^3-fibrations that are not Zariski-locally trivial, which disproves the Dolgachev–Weisfeiler conjecture over these bases. If it holds up, it settles the complex cancellation question in dimension four with a "no", and it knocks down two related conjectures along the way.

Do not say it is the first counterexample ever. Gupta already had counterexamples in positive characteristic in 2014. The new claim is over the complex numbers.
It is an AI-generated preprint, not a peer-reviewed, accepted result. Say 'the paper claims' or 'constructs'.
The fibration counterexamples are over the specific bases A^1 and A^2, in relative dimension 3, not in general.
Do not imply that the line bundle or the Lean component verifies the whole proof.

To show X is not 4-space, the paper rules out certain additive-group actions using a valuation along p=0 and the associated graded algebra, in the spirit of Makar-Limanov's proof for the Russell cubic.

problem_plain: Choose r random points in the plane and ask for a curve of degree d that passes through each point several times, like a knot looping back through it. Nagata's conjecture says that once there are 10 or more points this always costs a lot of degree: the total number of passes through the points must be less than d times the square root of r.
why_it_matters: Nagata posed it around 1959 while building his counterexample to Hilbert's fourteenth problem. It became a central open problem about curves through points, and it pins down a basic positivity invariant called the Seshadri constant.

history.fact: Nagata introduced the conjecture in his work on Hilbert's fourteenth problem and proved it when the number of points is a perfect square at least 16 (1959; 1965 reference also cited).

Partial bounds only: Roé (2001) proved d > m(sqrt(r-1) - pi/8) for r >= 10. For 10 points, Eckl (2011) and Ciliberto-Dumitrescu-Miranda-Roé (2011) proved d/m >= 117/37 (about 3.162), against the conjectured sqrt(10) (about 3.1623).
Ciliberto-Miranda-Roé (2026) constructed irrational square-zero nef rays for r >= 10. The paper notes that this does not determine the equal-weight Seshadri constant.

claim_precise: Theorem: for every r >= 10 there is a countable union E_r of proper Zariski-closed subsets of the space of r distinct points in P^2 over C such that, for every tuple outside E_r, every nonzero effective plane curve C of degree d >= 1 with mult_{p_i} C >= m_i satisfies d*sqrt(r) > sum m_i. This is the strict form with unequal multiplicities allowed, and it holds simultaneously for all curves, including reducible and nonreduced ones. As a consequence, the multipoint Seshadri constant of the plane at r very general points is 1/sqrt(r), and the result extends to uncountable algebraically closed fields of characteristic zero. Companion preprints in the same family claim maximal multipoint Seshadri constants (L^n/r)^{1/n} on any smooth polarized variety of dimension n >= 2 for all sufficiently large r: at very general points over C, and at the geometric generic tuple in positive characteristic.
claim_plain: The preprint claims a full proof of Nagata's conjecture: for 10 or more very general points, every plane curve's total multiplicity at the points is strictly less than its degree times the square root of the number of points. Follow-up preprints claim the analogous optimal Seshadri-constant statement in higher dimensions when there are enough points.
method_hint: The method slides the points onto a cubic curve, pushes the remaining points together along a line, and turns the existence of a too-good curve into a matrix that would have to lose rank. A polygon-counting interpolation argument then shows that the matrix has full rank.
overclaim_pitfalls: These are AI-generated preprints that have not yet been peer-reviewed. Say the paper claims a proof and avoid saying it has been settled.
The result is for very general points, not arbitrary points. Special point configurations can fail the inequality.
It does not hold for 9 or fewer points, because at 9 points a cubic always passes through all of them.
Nagata himself proved the perfect-square cases (r >= 16 square) in 1959, so only the non-square cases were open.
The higher-dimensional Seshadri results only claim 'sufficiently large r', not every r.
Do not say it solves Hilbert's fourteenth problem. Nagata already gave that counterexample in 1959.

problem_plain: Take any scattered set of points in the plane or in space, even a dusty fractal, and list every distance between two of its points. Falconer's question: if the set is "more than half-dimensional" (fractal dimension above d/2 in d-dimensional space), must that list of distances fill up a chunk of the number line with positive length?
why_it_matters: It is the continuous, fractal version of Erdős's distinct-distances problem and one of the central open problems of geometric measure theory and harmonic analysis, driving decades of work on Fourier restriction and decoupling.

history.fact: Falconer posed the problem in 1985, proving the distance set has positive length when the dimension exceeds (d+1)/2, and gave examples showing d/2 would be the sharp threshold.

In the plane the threshold improved from Falconer's 3/2 to Wolff's 4/3 (1999), and in 3D to 9/5 by Du, Guth, Ou, Wang, Wilson and Zhang (2021); for d>=4, Du and Zhang (2019) reached d/2 + 1/4 + 1/(8d-4).
