problem_plain: Take any region of the plane (or sphere) with holes in it, even infinitely many holes of any shape. Koebe asked in 1908 whether you can always smoothly reshape it, preserving all angles (a conformal map), so that every hole becomes a perfect round disk or a single point.
why_it_matters: Circle domains are the simplest possible models for planar regions, generalizing the Riemann mapping theorem from simply connected regions to all regions. Koebe's 'Kreisnormierungsproblem' has stood open for over a century in its general form.

history.fact: Koebe posed the circle-domain (Kreisnormierung) problem in 1908 and proved the finitely connected case (treatment of 1920).

He and Schramm (1993) proved the countably connected case (countably many holes), and proved rigidity for countably connected circle domains; in 1994 they extended rigidity to boundaries of sigma-finite length and conjectured rigidity iff the boundary is conformally removable.

Later partial results under geometric conditions: Karafyllia-Ntalampekos (2024, Gromov-hyperbolic domains), Esmayli-Rajala (2026, cospread domains); Rajala (2025) showed a rigid circle domain with non-removable boundary, refuting one direction of He-Schramm.

claim_precise: Paper 1 (Koebe's circle-domain conjecture): every nonempty connected open set G in the Riemann sphere is conformally equivalent to a circle domain (complementary components are closed round disks or points), with no restriction on the number (possibly uncountable) or geometry of complementary components. Paper 2 (Removable boundaries and rigidity): if Omega is a circle domain with conformally removable boundary, every conformal equivalence from Omega onto another circle domain is the restriction of a Möbius transformation — the removability-implies-rigidity direction of the He-Schramm conjecture (the converse direction was already shown false by Rajala 2025).
claim_plain: The preprints claim to settle the existence part of Koebe's 1908 conjecture in full: any region, with any number of holes of any shape, can be conformally reshaped so every hole is a round disk or a point. A companion paper claims that when the boundary is 'removable', this round model is unique up to Möbius transformations.
method_hint: Approximate by finitely-holed regions (where Koebe's theorem works), and use carefully chosen finite-energy 'test functions' (transboundary extremal length, after Schramm) to force every limiting hole to be either a point or exactly a round disk.
overclaim_pitfalls: Do not say it proves the full He-Schramm conjecture (rigidity iff removable): only removable => rigid is claimed; the converse is false (Rajala 2025).
Uniqueness/rigidity is not claimed for all circle domains, only those with conformally removable boundary.
Finite and countably many holes were already done by humans (Koebe 1920; He-Schramm 1993); the new claim is the general (uncountable, arbitrary) case.
These are AI-generated preprints, not peer-reviewed; say 'claims' rather than 'proved'.
It does not say every exhaustion's maps converge to a circle domain; only that a suitable exhaustion exists.

problem_plain: Picture a computer with only a tiny scratchpad of memory, just enough to write down a few positions in its input. If you let it flip coins, can it solve problems it otherwise couldn't, or can a version with no coins always do the same job in the same tiny memory?
why_it_matters: This is one of the central "does randomness help?" questions in complexity theory. Showing that L = BPL would mean randomness gives no extra power to memory-limited computation that runs in polynomial time.

history.fact: Aleliunas, Karp, Lipton, Lovász and Rackoff (1979) used random walks to solve undirected connectivity and explicitly asked whether randomized log-space could be simulated deterministically in log space.
Saks and Zhou (1999) showed bounded-error randomized log-space computation can be done deterministically in O(log^{3/2} n) space. Hoza (2021) improved this to O(log^{3/2} n / sqrt(log log n)).
Reingold (STOC 2005) settled the special case of undirected connectivity in deterministic log space.

claim_precise: Theorem 1: L = RL = BPL. Here RL and BPL are defined by randomized machines with polynomial worst-case running time and O(log n) work space, with one-sided error (RL) or two-sided bounded error (BPL). Theorem 2: for any such machine M, a deterministic algorithm given (x, 1^q) outputs M's acceptance probability on x to within 2^{-q}, using O(log n + q) space and (n+2)^{O(1)} 2^{O(q)} time. The paper also claims an effective compiler that turns a randomized source program, together with supplied time and space bounds, into a deterministic log-space decider with explicit resource bounds.
claim_plain: The paper claims that for log-space machines running in polynomial time, coin flips add no power: every such randomized machine can be replaced by a deterministic one that still uses only logarithmic memory. This is a preprint written by an AI model and has not yet been confirmed by the community.

Approximate it through a hierarchy of configuration copies, so that more than three quarters of a small, enumerable family of estimates are accurate. Then try every member of the family deterministically and go with the majority.

problem_plain: How fast can a computer multiply two huge n-digit numbers? Schoolbook long multiplication takes about n-squared steps, and for 50 years the conjectured speed limit has been about n times log n.
why_it_matters: Multiplication is one of the most basic operations in computing, and n log n was widely believed to be the true optimal cost; breaking it would overturn a conjecture from 1971.

history.fact: Karatsuba (with Ofman, 1962) beat schoolbook multiplication with O(n^{log2 3}) ~ n^1.585; Toom (1963) pushed to n^{1+eps} for every eps.
Schonhage and Strassen (1971) proved O(n log n log log n) on multitape Turing machines and proposed n log n as optimal; Furer (2007) improved to n log n 2^{O(log* n)}.
Harvey and van der Hoeven reached O(n log n) unconditionally (published 2021), matching the conjectured optimum.

claim_precise: There is a single deterministic multitape Turing machine (fixed finite alphabet, finitely many 1-D tapes) that exactly multiplies two n-bit integers for every n in worst-case time O(n (lg n)^{1-kappa}) with kappa = 2^{-182}. This refutes an Omega(n log n) lower bound (the Schonhage-Strassen optimality conjecture) in the ordinary multitape bit model. Constants and thresholds are astronomically large; the result is a theoretical bit-complexity bound, not a practical algorithm.
claim_plain: The AI-generated preprint claims a multiplication algorithm that is asymptotically a tiny bit faster than n log n, shaving a power of the log factor, which would disprove the 1971 conjecture that n log n is optimal on multitape Turing machines.
method_hint: Building on Harvey-van der Hoeven's Fourier-transform approach, it saves on both data shuffling and butterfly arithmetic by working with clever linear (XOR / sum-difference) combinations of the data instead of moving and processing each piece individually.

overclaim_pitfalls: Not a practical speedup: kappa = 2^{-182} and the constants are enormous, so it never helps real computers.
Does not mean multiplication is linear time; it only beats n log n by a minuscule power of log n.
The result is specific to the multitape Turing machine model; other models (e.g. Schonhage's storage-modification machines, linear time) already behaved differently.
It is an AI-generated preprint claim, not yet an established peer-reviewed result.
Do not say Harvey-van der Hoeven was wrong; their O(n log n) upper bound stands, only the conjecture that it is optimal is challenged.

problem_plain: Given a list of n whole numbers and a target, is there some selection of them that adds up exactly to the target? The obvious method tries all 2^n selections. The question is how much faster you can do it in the worst case.
why_it_matters: Subset Sum is one of the classic NP-complete problems. For about 50 years, no algorithm had brought the worst-case exponent below the 2^{n/2} barrier from 1974, so even a small fixed drop in the exponent is a notable change in the theory.

history.fact: Horowitz and Sahni (1974): meet-in-the-middle. Split the numbers in half, list each half's subset sums, and look for complementary pairs. This gives the 2^{n/2} time scale.
Schroeppel and Shamir (1981) kept the 2^{n/2} time while cutting the space to 2^{n/4}.
Chen, Jin, Randolph and Servedio (2023) got randomized O(2^{n/2} / n^{0.5023...}) time. That is only a polynomial-factor saving, and the exponent stays 1/2.

claim_precise: The paper claims a uniform randomized classical word-RAM algorithm for worst-case Subset Sum: n positive integers (repeats allowed) and a target, with bit length b polynomial in n and words of O(n+b) bits. It always halts and runs in at most C·2^{0.49n} word operations on every execution, and it answers correctly with probability at least 2/3 on every input. No assumption is made about how the inputs are distributed. The intermediate bound is 2^{0.489995n}·poly(n+b). A companion preprint gives a low-space algorithm for worst-case Subset Sum.
claim_plain: The paper claims the first worst-case Subset Sum algorithm that beats the 2^{n/2} meet-in-the-middle barrier in the exponent. Its running time is about 2^{0.49n}. The algorithm is randomized and is correct with high probability.
method_hint: The algorithm counts solutions modulo a random prime, using random phases (roots of unity) as a fingerprint. It then lists the false positives that the modulus creates ("aliases") and subtracts them out. An isolation step first arranges for exactly one true solution to remain.
overclaim_pitfalls: It does not prove P = NP and does not give a polynomial-time algorithm; the time is still exponential, 2^{0.49n}.
The gain is small (0.5 down to 0.49), so it is not a practical speedup.
It is randomized: correct with probability at least 2/3, not deterministic.
The result holds only for polynomial-bit inputs in a specific word-RAM model.
This is an AI-generated preprint that has not been peer reviewed; describe it as a claim.
Earlier 'faster' methods (Howgrave-Graham–Joux, Becker–Coron–Joux) worked only on random instances; this paper's claim is for the worst case.
visual_ideas: Meet-in-the-middle: split n dots into two halves, show two sorted columns of 2^{n/2} sums each, and draw matching lines between pairs that hit the target. Then a meter shows the exponent sliding from 0.50 to 0.49.
A clock of residues mod P: subset sums land on bins, the target bin lights up, and the aliases (wrong integer sums that share the bin) are struck out, leaving one true solution.

problem_plain: Borsuk asked whether any bounded shape in d-dimensional space can always be cut into d+1 pieces that are each strictly "narrower" (smaller diameter) than the whole. A disk works with 3 pieces and a ball works with 4, so it seemed natural that this should hold in every dimension.
why_it_matters: Borsuk's question is a famous example of low-dimensional intuition breaking down in high dimensions. Finding the smallest dimension where it fails is a long-running open problem, and a counterexample in dimension 9 would drop the known threshold from 63 to single digits.

history.fact: Borsuk posed the partition question in 1933; Kahn and Kalai disproved it in high dimensions in 1993.
Counterexample dimensions were pushed down over time: 946 (Nilli 1994), 561 (Raigorodskii 1997), 323 (Hinrichs 2002), 298 (Hinrichs-Richter 2003), 65 (Bondarenko 2014), 64 (Jenrich-Brouwer 2014).
The previous record the paper cites is dimension 63, from a finite counterexample in Grinsztajn's public proof note (2026).

claim_precise: Take X = {uu^T : u a unit vector in R^4}, the set of rank-one orthogonal projectors onto lines in R^4. It sits inside the 9-dimensional affine space of trace-one symmetric 4x4 matrices and uses the Frobenius metric. X is compact, has diameter sqrt(2), and cannot be covered by ten subsets of diameter strictly less than sqrt(2). So Borsuk's assertion (d+1 = 10 pieces) fails in dimension 9. A corollary extends this to compact counterexamples in every dimension d >= 9. The paper says explicitly that it does NOT determine the smallest dimension where Borsuk fails, and does not determine the exact Borsuk number of X.
claim_plain: This AI-generated preprint claims a 9-dimensional counterexample to Borsuk's conjecture: a shape built from all lines through the origin in 4D space that cannot be split into 10 narrower pieces. The best previously cited dimension was 63.
method_hint: Two points of the set are at maximum distance exactly when their lines are perpendicular. A topological degree argument on projective 3-space, combined with a finite combinatorial case analysis, then shows that 10 smaller pieces cannot avoid putting some pair of perpendicular lines into the same piece.
overclaim_pitfalls: Do not say 9 is the smallest dimension where Borsuk fails. The paper explicitly leaves that open, and dimensions 4 through 8 remain unresolved.
Do not say Borsuk's conjecture was 'disproved' for the first time. Kahn and Kalai disproved it in 1993; this claims a lower dimension.
This is an AI-generated preprint, not a peer-reviewed result. Say 'the paper claims'.
Do not claim the exact number of pieces needed for X is 11. The paper only shows that more than 10 are needed.
Do not say Borsuk's conjecture is false in dimension 3 or lower. It is true there (general knowledge).
visual_ideas: A disk split into 3 colored pieces and a ball into 4, each piece visibly narrower than the whole. Then show a 'dimension counter' ticking down through the record dimensions 946 -> 561 -> 323 -> 298 -> 65 -> 64 -> 63 before it drops to 9.

problem_plain: If one shape can fill all of space by sliding copies around, with no rotations, gaps or overlaps, can you always arrange those copies in a repeating, wallpaper-like pattern? The periodic tiling conjecture says yes.
why_it_matters: It asks whether a single tile can force non-repeating order. Dimension three is the lowest dimension where the answer could fail, because the conjecture is proved true in dimensions one and two.

history.fact: In one dimension, every tiling of the integers by one finite tile is periodic (Newman, 1977).
history.source: paper intro, 01-introduction.tex; Newman 1977 J. Number Theory

history.fact: Every finite tile of the 2D integer grid admits a periodic tiling (Bhattacharya, 2020).
history.source: paper intro, 01-introduction.tex; Bhattacharya 2020 Amer. J. Math.

history.fact: Greenfeld and Tao disproved the periodic tiling conjecture in some sufficiently large dimension (Annals of Mathematics, 2024), using a Sudoku-like encoding.

For lattice tilings, three is the smallest dimension where this can happen. The paper does not claim the tile is connected, and it does not claim that its tilings lack every individual period.

A 3D isometric stack of cubes in a disconnected tile shape filling a box. The pattern drifts as you scan upward and never repeats. Show a dashed 'period' arrow trying to match and failing with a red X.

problem_plain: Hadwiger's conjecture (1943) says that if a graph needs k colors to color it so no two neighbors share a color, then you can contract it down to k mutually-connected blobs, a complete graph K_k as a 'minor'. Put another way, needing many colors should always come with a big hidden clique structure.
why_it_matters: It is one of the central open problems in graph theory and a far-reaching generalization of the Four Color Theorem. Its K_5 case is equivalent to Four Color, and the K_6 case was proved by Robertson, Seymour and Thomas in 1993.

history.fact: Posed by Hadwiger in 1943. The K_4-minor-free case was proved by Hadwiger and Dirac (1952). The K_5 case is equivalent to the Four Color Theorem (Appel–Haken 1977). The K_6 case was proved by Robertson, Seymour and Thomas in 1993.

Best general upper bounds before this: O(t sqrt(log t)) colors (Kostochka, Thomason 1984), then O(t (log t)^beta) (Norin–Postle–Song 2023), then O(t log log t) (Delcourt–Postle 2025), and O(t log log log t) in a 2026 preprint by Liu–Luo.
Reed and Seymour (1998) proposed the fractional weakening chi_f(G) <= h(G) and proved it holds with a factor of 2.

claim_precise: The paper claims there are graphs of arbitrarily large order m with independence number at most 2 (among any 3 vertices, at least two are adjacent) whose largest connected matching has fewer than m/100 edges. As a result, h(G) < 26m/75 + 2/3 < m/2 <= chi_f(G) <= chi(G). This disproves Hadwiger's conjecture and also its fractional weakening chi_f <= h (Reed–Seymour 1998). It also disproves the Füredi–Gyárfás–Simonyi connected-matching conjecture. A companion paper uses the same kind of graphs to disprove the Colin de Verdière chromatic conjecture chi(G) <= mu(G)+1. A second companion paper proves the positive result chi_list(G) <= C·h(G) for an absolute constant C (the Linear List Hadwiger conjecture of Kawarabayashi–Mohar 2007), so chi(G) <= C·h(G).

If that holds, Hadwiger's conjecture is false. A companion preprint claims the conjecture is still true up to a constant factor: the number of colors is at most a fixed constant times the clique-minor size.

Missing edges are placed randomly so that pairs of potential matching edges keep 'conflicting', which keeps every connected matching, and therefore every clique minor, small.

problem_plain: Some infinite groups, viewed from very far away, have a "boundary at infinity". Cannon's conjecture says that if this boundary looks like an ordinary 2D sphere, the group must really be the symmetry group of a tiling of 3D hyperbolic space, as if it came from a hyperbolic 3-manifold.
why_it_matters: It would mean you can recognize hyperbolic 3D geometry purely from a group's large-scale shape. This makes it a central open problem connecting geometric group theory and 3-manifold topology.

history.fact: Cannon's 1994 combinatorial Riemann mapping theorem, then Cannon-Swenson (1998) stated the group-boundary conjecture; Cannon-Floyd-Parry (1999) reduced it to bounding discrete moduli of annuli.
Bonk-Kleiner proved the conjecture in the special case where the boundary's Ahlfors regular conformal dimension is attained.

Markovic gave a recognition criterion using quasiconvex surface subgroups. Groves-Haissinsky-Manning-Osajda-Sisto-Walsh showed that a relative version (the Toral Relative Cannon conjecture) implies a virtual Kleinian realization for residually finite such groups.

claim_precise: Theorem: if G is a word-hyperbolic group whose Gromov boundary is homeomorphic to S^2, then there is a homomorphism rho: G -> Isom(H^3) whose action on H^3 is proper and cocompact, with finite kernel (orientation-reversing isometries are allowed). Corollary: if G is torsion-free, G is the fundamental group of a closed hyperbolic 3-manifold, possibly nonorientable. The proof follows the analytic route. By the Bourdon-Kleiner criterion, it suffices to show that the combinatorial 2-modulus M(n) of fixed-scale coverings of the boundary stays bounded, and the paper argues by contradiction about how M(n) could grow.
claim_plain: This AI-generated preprint claims a full proof of Cannon's conjecture: any hyperbolic group whose boundary is a 2-sphere acts geometrically on hyperbolic 3-space. If it holds up, the torsion-free ones are exactly the fundamental groups of closed hyperbolic 3-manifolds.
overclaim_pitfalls: Do not call it an accepted or peer-reviewed resolution. It is an AI-generated preprint claiming a proof, and a famous decades-old conjecture needs expert verification.
Do not say it proves the Toral Relative Cannon conjecture or other related conjectures.

Do not claim every group with sphere boundary is exactly a 3-manifold group. Groups with torsion get the action only up to a finite kernel, and the manifold conclusion is only for torsion-free groups.
Do not credit the reduction to modulus bounds to this paper. That reduction is due to Cannon-Floyd-Parry and Bonk-Kleiner/Bourdon-Kleiner.

That makes the boundary conformally a round sphere, and the group's action can then be straightened into hyperbolic isometries.

problem_plain: The Partition Principle says that if you can split a set into pieces, there are never "more pieces than elements": you can always send the pieces one-to-one back into the original set. The Axiom of Choice (which lets you pick one element from every piece) clearly implies this, and the question was whether the reverse also holds, i.e. whether this size comparison is secretly as strong as full Choice.
why_it_matters: The question goes back to the early 1900s and is often called one of the oldest open problems in set theory. It asks whether comparing sizes of sets is really the same as being able to choose representatives.

history.fact: The paper, citing da Silva (2021), traces the Partition Principle to Beppo Levi in 1902.
It was classically known that the Partition Principle implies Choice for well-ordered (ordinal-indexed) families, an argument attributed to Pincus (recorded by Ryan-Smith, 2025).
Blass and Kulshreshtha's August 2026 version still listed 'Partition Principle implies Choice?' as open.

claim_precise: If ZF is consistent, then so is ZF + Partition Principle + Choice for ordinal-indexed families + not-AC. Separately, starting from any countable transitive model of ZFC, the paper builds a transitive symmetric submodel of a forcing extension with the same ordinals that satisfies ZF + PP + AC for well-orderable families + not-AC and adds no new countable sequences of ground-model elements.
claim_plain: The paper claims a negative answer: it builds a mathematical universe where the Partition Principle holds but the Axiom of Choice fails. So the Partition Principle does not imply Choice (assuming ordinary set theory is consistent).
method_hint: Build a symmetric model around a special set A of generic subsets of omega_1 that cannot be well-ordered, arranged so that every non-well-orderable image of A is in bijection with A itself. That makes reverse injections exist everywhere, even though choice fails.
overclaim_pitfalls: Do not say it proves the Axiom of Choice false. It shows Choice cannot be derived from PP in ZF; Choice is still consistent too.
It is a relative consistency result: it assumes ZF is consistent.
Do not say PP is 'useless' or weak. PP still implies choice for well-ordered families.
It is an AI-generated preprint; say 'the paper claims' rather than calling it settled or peer-reviewed.

problem_plain: Picture a ring of tiny quantum magnets ("spin-one" particles), where each one wants to point opposite to its neighbors. Haldane predicted that adding the smallest possible amount of energy to such a chain always costs a fixed minimum, which does not shrink to zero however long the ring gets. history.fact: Haldane formulated the prediction in 1981 and published it in 1983. It says integer-spin antiferromagnetic chains have a gap and half-odd-integer chains do not.

problem_plain: Picture stirring a drop of dye into a glass of water. "Mixing" means that after a long time, any patch of the glass holds its fair share of the dye. Rokhlin asked whether this two-moment kind of mixing automatically gives mixing among three or more far-apart moments in time, so that every collection of events becomes independent once the gaps between them grow large.
why_it_matters: This is one of the oldest open questions in ergodic theory, about 75 years old. It asks whether the simplest form of randomness in a dynamical system already forces all the higher forms.

history.fact: Rokhlin introduced higher-order mixing in 1949, proved it for certain group endomorphisms, and asked whether mixing implies mixing of higher orders.

problem_plain: C*-algebras are systems of infinite matrices (operators) that come with a built-in "mirror" operation, the adjoint, and the question is whether any well-behaved (bounded) way of representing them as operators can be fixed by a single change of coordinates, so that the mirror operation is respected too. Put differently: if a representation only respects multiplication, can you always tilt the geometry of the space so that it respects the adjoint as well?
why_it_matters: It is one of the oldest open problems in operator algebras, the mathematics behind quantum mechanics. Over decades it was shown to be equivalent to many other statements, for example about derivations and about "hyperreflexivity" of von Neumann algebras, so settling it would settle all of those at once.

history.fact: Posed by Richard Kadison in 1955.

Previously solved only in special cases: nuclear C*-algebras (Bunce, Christensen, 1981), cyclic representations and algebras without tracial states (Haagerup, 1983), and II_1 factors with property Gamma (Christensen, 1986).
Haagerup (1983) showed that similarity to a *-representation is equivalent to complete boundedness; Kirchberg (1996) showed the problem is equivalent to every derivation being inner.

There are no separability, nuclearity or other assumptions. The key step is a uniform commutator estimate: there is an absolute constant C with ||[Y^(h), X]|| <= C g_P(Y) ||X|| for every von Neumann algebra P, every operator Y, every matrix size h, and every X in M_h(P). As a corollary, every von Neumann algebra is hyperreflexive with constant at most 2C. No bound on the condition number of S is claimed, and the paper does not claim C is optimal.

problem_plain: Given any linear transformation T of an infinite-dimensional space (other than multiplying by a fixed number), is there always some nontrivial "room" (a closed subspace other than zero and the whole space) that T maps into itself, and that every transformation that commutes with T also maps into itself? This is the "hyperinvariant subspace problem", a stronger version of the famous invariant subspace problem.
why_it_matters: The invariant subspace problem is one of the best-known open questions in operator theory. The hyperinvariant version was a natural stronger version of it, and a "no" answer shows that the two questions really are different.

history.fact: Douglas and Pearcy (1972) studied how hyperinvariant subspaces relate to transitive operator algebras.
Arveson (1967) density theorem: a transitive algebra on separable Hilbert space that contains a maximal abelian self-adjoint subalgebra is strongly dense in B(H).
Atzmon and Sodin (1999) built completely indecomposable bilateral weighted shifts and left open whether they have proper hyperinvariant subspaces.

Equivalently, its commutant {S}' is a proper, strongly closed, unital, transitive operator algebra, which also answers negatively whether every unital transitive operator algebra is strongly dense in B(H). The operator is a field of weighted shifts over the 2-adic integers, and it still has many ordinary invariant subspaces. So the classical invariant subspace problem is NOT resolved. A companion paper answers a question of Zhu, Fang and Shi: for every irrational rotation angle theta, it builds a continuous weight f such that the operator U f(V) in the hyperfinite II_1 factor R_theta has no nontrivial invariant projection in that factor. These are AI-generated preprints.

history.fact: Hilbert's fifth problem (1900) asked how far differentiability could be dropped in continuous transformation groups; Gleason and Montgomery-Zippin resolved the locally Euclidean group version in 1952.

problem_plain: Plug a matrix into a polynomial and you get a new matrix. How big can it be? Crouzeix's conjecture says it is never more than twice the polynomial's largest size on a region called the matrix's "numerical range". The "complete" version asks whether the same factor 2 still works when the polynomial's coefficients are themselves matrices, no matter how large those matrices are.
why_it_matters: For non-normal matrices, the eigenvalues alone say almost nothing about how functions of the matrix behave. The numerical range gives a guaranteed bound, and that matters for stability and convergence in numerical linear algebra and operator theory.

history.fact: Crouzeix posed the constant-two question in 2004 and proved a universal (complete) bound of 11.08 in 2007.
Crouzeix and Palencia (2017) improved the complete bound to 1 + sqrt(2), about 2.414.

Ahag, Czyz and Virtanen (2026) handle the complete case for matrices of size at most 3.

problem_plain: The Allen-Cahn equation models two mixed phases, like oil and water, separating with a smooth transition layer between them. De Giorgi asked: if a solution steadily increases in one direction, is its transition layer forced to be perfectly flat, with every level set a parallel plane, at least in dimensions up to eight?

Savin (2009) proved it up to dimension 8, but only under an extra assumption that the solution tends to -1 and +1 at the two ends of every line in the monotone direction.
Del Pino, Kowalczyk and Wei (2011) built non-flat monotone solutions in every dimension 9 and above, so 8 is the sharp endpoint.

problem_plain: A closed geodesic is a loop on a curved surface or space that is "locally straightest", like a rubber band that has snapped tight around a lumpy ball.
